extracted.intended_audience: government attorneys, military legal advisers, tax officials, and administrators handling taxation of federal instrumentalities and territorial law
extracted.subtask_description: Legal/practical standards governing when States, Territories, or municipalities may tax or charge fees to United States officers, instrumentalities, property, and military activities, with examples and citations. Includes rules about reservations, exclusive jurisdiction, inspections, assessments, and related territorial law.

rubrics_metrics.name: State taxation of Federal officers' compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: A State statute may not tax the office or salary of an officer of the United States; compensation is fixed by Congress and a State law that diminishes that recompense conflicts with federal law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leading case: Dobbins v. Commissioners of Erie County (16 Peters, 435). Courts hold State laws imposing taxes upon the office or salary of federal officers are unconstitutional because they interfere with compensation fixed by Congress. (See citations: Society for Savings v. Coite; multiple Attorney General opinions and later cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: No State tax on instruments/emoluments/persons essential to federal powers
rubrics_metrics.description: A State cannot lay a tax upon the instruments, emoluments, and persons which the United States may use and employ as necessary and proper means to execute their sovereign powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General doctrinal principle repeated in many cases (e.g., McCulloch v. Maryland; Railroad Co. v. Peniston; Van Brocklin v. Tennessee). State tax laws cannot abridge the operation of constitutionally valid federal laws or restrain federal action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional authorization can allow taxation of federal supplies
rubrics_metrics.description: An instrumentality of the United States may be taxed by a State or Territory if Congress has authorized such taxation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Acts of August 5, 1909 authorized imposition of customs duties and internal-revenue taxes on supplies imported into the Philippine Islands for Army use (C. 2747, Mar. 11, 1911).

rubrics_metrics.name: Retired officers' pay exempt but other property taxable
rubrics_metrics.description: The exemption from taxation of an officer's office or salary applies equally to retired officers on the retired list; retired officers are part of the Army machinery and their Army pay is not taxable by State or municipal authorities, but other personal property they own remains taxable like any other citizen's property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited opinions: R. 36, 154; various Comptroller/Attorney General decisions (C. 14582; R. 42, 669). Enlisted men on retired list similarly treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poll tax with compulsory labor alternative invalid against military personnel
rubrics_metrics.description: Imposition of a poll tax with the alternative that nonpayment requires working on the road is a tax on the earnings or time of an active-duty officer or soldier and therefore cannot lawfully be imposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal taxation of officers for non-military property
rubrics_metrics.description: Although officers or soldiers are not taxable officially on account of their Army pay or military instruments/implements, they may be personally taxable for household furniture and other non-military personal property (except where stationed on land under exclusive federal jurisdiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See opinions R. 53, 598; C. 3574; and related citations. Local law applies to non-military personal property when not on exclusively federal land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residence for taxation requires personal intent; stationing not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Residence (for tax/residency purposes) is a matter of personal intent; being commorant at a military station by order does not, by itself, establish residency in the State or Territory where the station is located.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because military presence is involuntary and temporary and subject to change by orders, it is generally presumed not to be the soldier's residence. (Citations: R. 30, 215; R. 37, 396; C. 3574; C. 14852.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Former soldiers/pensioners not federally exempt from State taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no provision in U.S. law that relieves former soldiers, pensioners, or inmates of National Homes from State taxation (per capita taxes, property taxes), unless the State itself has enacted a specific exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities: P. 60, 325; C. 2513; various Comptroller/AG opinions. Likewise, being a discharged soldier or pensioner does not federally excuse payment of road tax or road labor except where State law provides exemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: No federal exemption from local license fees for ex-soldiers selling goods
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no federal statute exempting ex-soldiers of the regular or volunteer service from paying usual license fees for selling or peddling goods under State or municipal laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authority: C. 17962, May 3, 1905; Apr. 16, 1908; Dec. 11, 1911.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal officers on federal reservations cannot be compelled to work or be imprisoned for unpaid State taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: A superintendent of a national cemetery (and analogous federal officers) cannot be imprisoned or compelled to work on roads for failure to pay a State tax levied by State authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 29377, Jan. 17, 1912; principle derives from exemption of federal instrumentalities from certain state processes when those would interfere with federal operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial employer obligation to furnish list/pay school tax — limited by federal interests
rubrics_metrics.description: A Territorial law requiring employers to furnish names and pay school tax for employees may be applied to government employees residing on a reservation unless it appears that imposition would adversely affect a United States instrumentality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: C. 23343, June 6, 1908 and June 9, 1909. Practical recommendation: where service by a territorial agency affects federal functions, place on contractual basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: State cession of exclusive jurisdiction need not expressly relinquish tax power; federal means remain untaxable
rubrics_metrics.description: When a State cedes exclusive jurisdiction over a military reservation, the State's statute need not specifically relinquish tax power; independently the State lacks power to tax means employed by Congress to perform federal functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority: P. 64, 330, Apr. 9, 1894; related cases apply McCulloch v. Maryland principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preexisting tax liens on land conveyed to US are not enforceable against US property after exclusive jurisdiction vests
rubrics_metrics.description: If taxes are a lien upon land when it is conveyed to the United States and exclusive jurisdiction is subsequently vested in the United States, those taxes are not enforceable against United States property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 1838, May 14, 1906. Principle protects federal property from local enforcement of prior liens once federal jurisdiction attaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: State reservation of power to tax persons/corporations doing business on reservation can be constitutional
rubrics_metrics.description: An act ceding jurisdiction over a military reservation may reserve to the State power to tax persons and corporations doing business on the reservation, and such a reservation of power can be constitutional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 27365, Oct. 15, 1910; depends on the precise terms of the cession and whether federal operations are interfered with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of exclusive federal jurisdiction permits State license taxes (e.g., canteens)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where exclusive jurisdiction has not been ceded by the State over a military reservation, State authorities may legally levy license taxes for activities such as selling beer at a post canteen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: R. 50, 153 (Mar. 30, 1886) re Sidney Barracks; P. 36, 161 (Oct. 29, 1889) re Fort Mackinac canteen. Distinguish post exchange (federal instrumentality) from canteen operations where state jurisdiction remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private improvements on leased federal park lands taxable if State retains jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Parcels within a national park leased for building purposes, where the State never ceded exclusive jurisdiction, may be assessed and taxed by the State as private property (improvements by lessees are taxable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mackinac National Park improvements taxed as private property (P. 39, 89, Feb. 26, 1890).

rubrics_metrics.name: Property conveyed for federal depot is an instrumentality exempt from local taxation and assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: Land conveyed to the United States for federal depot purposes is an instrumentality of the federal government and is not subject to local taxation of any kind, including assessments for street improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 2598, Sept. 10, 1896; C. 8272; C. 10094. Comptroller and courts have consistently applied McCulloch v. Maryland to bar such local impositions; Congress usually refuses appropriations to pay such assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: US not liable for municipal assessments for certain adjacent improvements, but must pay for use of town-owned facilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States is not liable for municipal assessments for construction of sewers, water pipes, or street improvements adjacent to federal property; however, if the US desires to use a sewer or other town-owned facility, it must pay for the privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: C. 3930; C. 13428; C. 6831 (June 24, 1902). Distinguish between compulsory assessments (non-liability) and voluntary use of local services (payment required).

rubrics_metrics.name: US not liable for certain local consumption taxes on supplies for troops (territorial nuance)
rubrics_metrics.description: In certain territorial contexts, the United States was held not liable for consumption taxes imposed locally on goods (e.g., sugar purchased in Porto Rico for US troops).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 6054, Mar. 18, 1899 — illustrates nuance in insular/territorial taxation rules; context-specific and may depend on local law and federal policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local inspection/permit fees claimed against US operations are taxation and generally not payable; contract recommended
rubrics_metrics.description: Fees charged by territorial or state authorities for inspection or regulatory services (e.g., animal inspectors, boiler inspections, electrical installation inspections) on federal operations are in effect taxes on federal instrumentalities and cannot legally be paid; if the service is valuable to the US, it should be procured by contract and paid at lawful rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple examples: C. 5554, C. 5551 (Dec. 31, 1909; Jan. 6, 1910); C. 18351 (July 28, 1905); C. 21469 (Apr. 24, 1907). Recommendation: place services on contractual basis limited to statutory rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charges against Army transports for quarantine/harbor inspection are taxes and cannot be imposed; contracting possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempted charges against Army transports for quarantine inspection or harbor regulation constitute taxes on federal instrumentalities and cannot be imposed; while States may establish quarantine and port regulations under their police power, no charge may be levied on the US unless there is a contract to pay an agreed amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: C. 20564 (Oct. 27 and Nov. 13, 1906); application includes foreign-occupied contexts (e.g., Cuba) — inspections required but fees should not be charged absent contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: State quarantine powers may not be used to impede movement of US troops
rubrics_metrics.description: A State may not exert its police power in quarantine matters in a way that interferes with the movement or operations of United States troops; claims arising from such interference are not proper charges against the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claim for health certificates charged against soldiers in transit denied (U. 6339, May 1, 1899).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal officers conducting authorized sales not subject to merchant licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer of the Army acting under federal authority to sell government property (e.g., damaged medical supplies under section 1241, R. S.) cannot be required to obtain or pay for a State merchant license for such sales, as that would unconstitutionally restrict federal functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 39, 6, May 8, 1876; principle prevents state regulation from restricting lawful execution of federal powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: No State or DC license fee on Government vehicles
rubrics_metrics.description: States and the District of Columbia may not lawfully impose license fees on government automobiles or vehicles used in the service of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 25127 (multiple dates 1909–1911) and C. 28165 (Apr. 24, 1911) — consistent holdings against licensing fees on federal vehicles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post exchanges selling exclusively to military personnel are exempt from local taxes/licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: A post exchange (retail operation) that exists as an instrumentality of the federal government and sells commodities exclusively for the use of persons in the military service is not legally liable for local or municipal taxes or licenses on those sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 7324, Nov. 21, 1899; distinguishes post exchanges (federal instrumentality) from private vendors operating on or near posts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial statutes operative on reservations unless conflicting with federal law or military administration
rubrics_metrics.description: A Territorial statute is operative upon a military reservation within the Territory so long as it does not conflict with United States law or the legitimate operations and administration of the military government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Arizona statute penalizing sale of liquor to Indians would not legally affect sale to enlisted soldiers when Army regulations permit such sales (various citations P. 48, 464; C. 12700; C. 14335).

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial governments cannot tax federal instrumentalities without legislation; prefer contractual arrangement for services
rubrics_metrics.description: The government of a Territory cannot, unaided by Congressional legislation, impose a tax upon a United States instrumentality; where territorial agencies render services necessary to federal operations, the service should be provided under contract and compensation limited to statutory rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 21469, Apr. 24, 1907; policy/practical guidance for interactions between territorial authorities and federal agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military must obey territorial district court subpoenas that substantially conform to federal forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Military personnel should obey subpoenas of district courts of Territories where those subpoenas, under relevant statutes (sections 877 and 911, R. S.), substantially conform to prescribed forms and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 54, 124 (July, 1887); C. 1469, Apr. 24, 1907 — applies to subpoenas in territorial district courts vested with federal jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Posse Comitatus inoperative in Alaska; marshal and commanding officer roles
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute (act of June 6, 1900), the Posse Comitatus Act is made inoperative in Alaska; the U.S. marshal determines the necessity for military force and the commanding officer assists and directs employment of troops to accomplish marshal's purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 3119 (Feb. 13 and Apr. 1, 1907) — operational rule for use of military forces in Alaska under territorial arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency sales to civilians in Alaska permitted at net cost and must be reported to Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: When emergency humanitarian needs require sale of small amounts of government coal to civilians in Alaska (surplus beyond military needs), such sales may be made at net cost, delivered at place of sale, but should be reported to Congress at its next session.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 19307 (Mar. 2 and Oct. 13, 1906) — example of constrained exception permitting limited civilian transactions.
